sources.news_title: 'Human vs. Robot' cage match was a hit. Sports commission calls a foul
'Human vs. Robot' cage match was a hit. State says event was illegal, but organizers aren't concerned
sources.text:
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Influencer Frankie LaPenna beat two of three remotely operated humanoid robots in a San Francisco cage match. Videos have drawn more than 10 million YouTube views.
- California’s State Athletic Commission says the Sept. 18 spectacle required its approval and issued organizers a cease-and-desist order, warning that unlicensed combat events are illegal.
- The event’s organizer argues the law applies to contests between people, not robots.
A human defeated two of the three robots he faced in a cage fight recently held in San Francisco.
The humans behind that fight could face a battle of their own — the legal type — if they want to hold another event like “Human Vs. Robot,” the Sept. 18 competition that placed influencer Frankie LaPenna inside an octagon to battle three humanoid robots that were controlled remotely by a human operator in separate MMA-style fights.
REK (Robot Entertainment Kombat), the “humanoid robot fighting” company that staged the event, billed it as the “first human vs. robot fight in history.” Videos of the bouts have combined for more than 10 million views on YouTube.
Lightning, one of more than 100 robots running the Beijing E-Town, avoided a serious mishap and crossed the finish line in a record 50 minutes, 26 seconds.
Not everyone is a fan. On Sept. 23, the California State Athletic Commission sent a cease-and-desist order to REK, its CEO Cix Liv and “all persons holding, promoting, advertising or sponsoring unsanctioned human versus humanoid robot cage fight.”
The letter states that “any boxing or mixed martial arts contest, match, or exhibition, involving any human in the State of California” requires the prior approval of the commission and that it is a misdemeanor to hold such an event without obtaining a license or permit from the state.
A spokesperson for the California Department of Consumer Affairs, which oversees the CSAC, said in a statement emailed to The Times that the commission is “committed to protecting the safety of the public and integrity of combat sports.”
“Unsanctioned activity puts the physical and financial well-being of all those involved at risk and such activity will not be tolerated,” the statement said.
An X post by Liv on Sept. 30 indicated he’s not overly concerned about the cease-and-desist order.
“We made it boys,” he wrote in the post, which also included a photo of the commission’s letter.
Liv said in an email to The Times on Tuesday that REK did not seek CSAC approval before the event “because the law clearly states it is not a real boxing match if it doesn’t include ‘two persons,’” rather than a human vs. a humanoid robot controlled by a human.
“So they can argue in court that actuators are somehow persons,” he said. “The case would give us nonstop media coverage, even if we incurred a fine.”
On the heels of an AI-powered humanoid robot setting the world record in the half-marathon, a study reveals that AI robots have defeated elite players in table tennis.
LaPenna also appeared to make light of the cease-and-desist order in a pair of X posts on Oct. 1.
“I fought a robot and within 12 days the state of California passes a new law saying no more robot vs. human fights,” wrote LaPenna, who did not immediately respond to a request for comment for this article.
He added in the second post: “Good work Cix, you disrupted the system.”
According to Liv, LaPenna pushed for the opportunity to face humanoid opponents in the cage.
Faraday Future, a high-end electric vehicle company, is moving its focus to AI and humanoid robots that could aid in education, housework and companionship.
“We felt the robots were ready to fight amateur fighters like Frankie, but not actual MMA fighters yet,” Liv said.
The 29-year-old content creator signed a full waiver of liability, but “we didn’t actually want to hurt him,” Liv added.
The written description accompanying a “Human vs. Robot” video posted on REK and LaPenna’s YouTube pages states that “there was no predetermined outcome, both Frankie and Nick, the robot operator were told to try their best.”
Wearing spiked gloves, a helmet and protective padding, the 5-foot-6, 205-pound LaPenna held his own against all three bots. He dominated his first opponent, referred to at the fight as “the child robot.” Next came an imposing “Terminator”-inspired humanoid, which was listed on the fight video as 6-feet and 200 pounds with a kick force of 850 pounds.
The robot landed several hard kicks, including one that knocked LaPenna across the mat and another with an impact that brought the humanoid to the ground and caused its head to come off — but the human seemed to gain strength as the match went on and eventually stood triumphantly with his foot on the machine’s crumpled body.
LaPenna was dominant early in his final match, in which he faced a robot that resembled a “Predator” from the movies of the same name. After landing several punches and kicks and taking his opponent to the ground multiple times, LaPenna eventually became fatigued and called for the match to be ended.
“He doesn’t get tired. He doesn’t stay down,” LaPenna said in a postmatch interview. “Just keeps getting up. I thought he’d be dead.”
Nine months after a quick injury sealed Joshua Van’s win over Alexande Pantoja, Van won the rematch during UFC 331 at Crypto.com Arena Saturday.
According to Liv, LaPenna emerged from the bouts basically unscathed. “The only damage he experienced was hurting his hand a bit by punching metal,” Liv said.
Since then, REK has turned its attention back to all-robot fights, although Liv said the company eventually plans to stage more human vs. humanoid bouts.
“We are avoiding it for now,” Liv said. “CSAC has no legal case but it may not be worth the battle. We may just do it in Vegas or a state that is less lame.”

sources.news_title: California Clamps Down on Human vs. Humanoid Cage Fights
sources.text:
A 6-foot machine with a Terminator-style head slammed its foot into Frankie LaPenna’s face. The influencer flew backward into the cage wall. Moments later, another kick sent him crashing to the mat. The San Francisco crowd of roughly 100 cheered wildly. Yet that September 18 bout has now drawn the full weight of state regulators.
The California State Athletic Commission issued a cease-and-desist letter days later. It ordered Robot Entertainment Kombat, known as REK, and its CEO Cix Liv to stop any unsanctioned events involving humans. The company celebrated. Liv posted the letter on X with a simple message: “We made it boys.”
The Human-Robot Clash That Crossed a Line
REK bills itself as the humanoid robot fighting league. Its events feature machines often built on platforms like EngineAI, modified with aggressive heads and piloted remotely via virtual-reality systems. In the September fight, LaPenna faced multiple robots. One delivered punches that dropped him. Another child-sized unit offered less resistance. The main event, however, left LaPenna with a hand injury and generated REK’s most-viewed clip to date. (The New York Times)
But California law draws a sharp boundary. Any boxing, kickboxing or mixed martial arts contest, match or exhibition involving a human requires prior approval and licensing from the commission. The cease-and-desist, signed by Executive Officer Andy Foster, made the violation clear. It declared the September 18 event unsanctioned. Promoting or participating without a license constitutes a misdemeanor under Business and Professions Code sections 18640, 18870 and 18878. The letter demanded an immediate halt. (The Verge)
Liv shows little concern. He has framed the regulatory pushback as validation. REK opened a San Francisco storefront earlier this year. There, visitors can watch, train with, repair and even purchase humanoid robots. The company had hosted robot-versus-robot bouts for over a year before escalating to human opponents. Those earlier matches drew participants who ranked in online simulators and competed for standings. Yet the human element changed everything.
Short. Direct. The state sees risk. A teleoperated robot can generate forces far beyond a human fist. One kick felt like a motorized bat traveling at high speed, Liv once remarked in an interview with local media. Liability questions multiply. Insurance. Safety standards. Medical oversight. None appeared present in the warehouse bout.
And the company plans to push forward anyway. REK scheduled its “Deathmatch” for October 9 in San Francisco. Three fights pit 6-foot humanoids against each other. This time, the machines carry weapons. Spartan Blades and Claw Blades arm the combatants. Promotional material promises a world-first humanoid weapon fight. Tickets started at $69 for general admission. The card includes a G1 weapon bout, a T800 matchup and a main event between Rektile and T-REK. Liv joked on X, “Our robot fights were too dangerous, so we put swords on them.” (Dexerto)
REK’s stated goal sounds almost noble on the surface. “We’re going to democratize MMA so we can essentially experience the blood sport without anyone getting hurt,” Liv told reporters. The violence stays between machines. Humans watch safely from outside the cage. Yet the September event proved the line blurs fast. One human stepped inside. Regulators noticed immediately.
Broader Questions for a Growing Industry
This episode arrives as humanoid robots gain real capabilities. Companies worldwide pour resources into machines that walk, balance, grasp and now strike with force. REK collects impact data during fights. It tests balance recovery in real time. The bouts serve as both spectacle and engineering validation. Yet they also expose gaps in oversight.
State athletic commissions exist to protect participants and maintain standards in combat sports. Their rules assumed human opponents. A remotely piloted robot complicates that framework. Who bears responsibility when a machine injures a human? The pilot? The company? The venue? Current statutes offer limited guidance. The commission’s letter sidesteps robot-only events. Its language targets only contests involving any human. Pure machine fights appear exempt for now. (USA Today)
REK has events listed in multiple cities, including Los Angeles, Palo Alto and international spots such as Tokyo and Vancouver. The San Francisco area remains its stronghold. The Van Ness storefront doubles as showroom and training ground. Customers learn to walk the machines, program basic behaviors and perform repairs. Liv once compared the experience to early fighting-game arcades. The spectacle draws crowds. The technology improves with each match.
Critics see darker undertones. Videos of robots pummeling a human influencer evoke dystopian imagery. One clip showed a rapid series of face punches. Another kick to the stomach left LaPenna sprawled. The crowd loved it. Online viewers reached millions. Yet the physical toll on the human participant raises ethical flags. Even if future events eliminate human fighters, the normalization of violent robot combat invites scrutiny.
So far, REK shows no sign of slowing. Its latest promotions lean into the drama. Red-and-blue artwork. Fighting-game character energy. Liv has signaled interest in semi-autonomous operation rather than full independence. “Fully autonomous isn’t as fun,” the company posted on X. The human pilot remains central. That choice keeps the fights entertaining. It also keeps regulatory questions alive.
The September 18 bout lasted long enough to produce lasting footage. LaPenna absorbed real damage. The robot demonstrated closed-loop balance after attacks. Data flowed back to engineers. For REK, the night delivered both content and progress. For California officials, it crossed a statutory line. The cease-and-desist arrived quickly. Whether it deters future human involvement remains uncertain. The October 9 Deathmatch proceeds without humans in the cage. Blades, however, introduce new hazards. Sparks. Flying metal. Potential for machines to damage each other spectacularly.
Industry watchers note the pattern. Entertainment drives adoption. Robot combat echoes historical spectacles from gladiators to monster trucks. Yet the machines evolve. What starts as remote-controlled theater could edge toward greater autonomy. When that shift occurs, liability and safety rules will need rewriting. Until then, REK operates in a gray zone. It courts attention. It collects data. And it dares regulators to keep up.
Recent coverage highlights the tension. Some outlets frame the story as regulatory overreach in a nascent field. Others warn of unchecked risks in a city already grappling with rapid tech expansion. No major updates have emerged since the letter became public. The Deathmatch event, if it occurs as planned, will test whether robot-only combat draws similar attention. For now, REK has turned state disapproval into marketing gold. “We made it boys” reads less like surrender and more like a battle cry.

The California State Athletic Commission sent a cease-and-desist letter to a startup that hosted a match between a human and a robot last month, as reported by The New York Times.
California is trying to shut down robot vs. human cage matches
The state says Rek, the ‘humanoid robot fighting league,’ can’t host fights involving ‘any human’ in California without permission.
The fight, which took place on September 18th, pitted a human, Frankie LaPenna, against a humanoid robot owned by a tech startup, Rek, that was being piloted by a human using what the NYT described as a “remote virtual-reality system.” Rek says it is the “the humanoid robot fighting league” on its website, and the robot appears to be one from EngineAI but with a Terminator-like head swapped on top.
You can watch a replay of the fight on YouTube:
The CEO of Rek, Cix Liv, posted the letter to X on September 30th, which called the fight “unsanctioned” and demanded that Liv and REK stop “holding, promoting or advertising any boxing or mixed martial arts contest match, or exhibition, involving any human” in California without the approval of the California State Athletic Commission. “We made it boys,” Liv said.

sources.news_title: California Cracks Down On Man Vs. Robot Fight Nights
sources.text:
A California athletic commission sent a cease-and-desist letter to a San Francisco tech startup after it staged a cage fight between a man and three humanoid robots.
On September 18, social media influencer Frankie LaPenna fought three remote-controlled robots in front of 100 cheering spectators. Two of the robots stood about 6 feet tall, with steel frames. Five days later, the California State Athletic Commission (CSAC) sent the letter to the organizer, Robot Entertainment Kombat (REK).
“We made it boys,” Cix Liv, CEO of REK, posted to X with a photo of the letter attached. “California sent us a Cease and Desist for ‘UNSANCTIONED HUMAN VERSUS HUMANOID ROBOT CAGE FIGHT.’”
View this post on Instagram
In the letter, the commission said it must approve boxing or mixed martial arts events involving a human and that holding an unsanctioned event was a misdemeanor.
“Unsanctioned activity puts the physical and financial well-being of all those involved at risk and such activity will not be tolerated,” the commission said in a statement.
Liv argued that REK — which describes itself as “the humanoid robot fighting league” — did not need the commission’s approval.
“The law clearly states that a ‘match’ is between two persons,” he said in an interview, according to The New York Times. He also said state regulators were welcome to try to prove that a humanoid robot was human.
Before the fight, LaPenna, who injured his hand at the event, signed a waiver stating that the company would not be held liable if he were killed. According to the Times, LaPenna had repeatedly asked REK to let him fight its robots.
“Our hope was to basically get some good shots without actually hurting Frankie,” Liv said.
The company, which has also organized robot fights in Canada and Japan, is hosting what it calls the “world’s first humanoid weapon fight” in San Francisco on Friday. That event will pit robots against one another, with no human combatants.
Humanoid robots are a growing sector of the technology industry. This summer, the second annual World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing featured more than 2,000 robots and 666 teams competing in sports including soccer, running, and table tennis.

sources.news_title: Influencer Takes on Robot in Cage Match in Latest Proof We’re Heading Toward ‘The Terminator’ in Real Life
That Humanoid Fighting Robot Startup on Van Ness Just Got a Cease and Desist From the State
sources.text:
After a video went viral of an obviously dangerous cage match between a human and a humanoid robot, California state officials have ordered San Francisco-based Robot Entertainment Kombat to cease all such unlicensed cage fights.
Robot Entertainment Kombat (REK), which just opened a storefront on Van Ness in July, is arguably one of the more bro-ishly frightening and dystopian developments on the local AI scene. The company had been marketing robot-on-robot fights for entertainment purposes, but then they got influencer Frankie LaPenna to don some (fairly minimal?) protective gear and have a cage fight last month with a six-foot-tall, Terminator-style robot.
To save you the viewing if you haven't clicked play already or haven't seen this on your feed, LaPenna gets his ass kicked, quite literally — every time the robot kicks he goes flying and it is nowhere near a fair fight.
LaPenna is best known for goofy stunt content on TikTok, and for going on America's Got Talent to pop some balloons with his big ass.
And in addition to the fight seen above, LaPenna also fought an REK robot called The Predator, which is allegedly made of "solid steel," and he does slightly better it looks like but still get his ass kicked in the end. (REK apparently claimed that LaPenna won two out of three of his matches that night, but did he? It kind of feels like we all lost something here.)
Needless to stay, state officials are not too happy about this new form of entertainment. As Tom's Hardware reported over the weekend, REK received a cease-and-desist letter from the California State Athletic Commission following the September 18 cage matches.
The letter, which REK CEO Cix Liv proudly shared on Xitter, orders REK to stop "holding, promoting, or advertising any boxing or mixed martial arts contest match or exhibition, involving any human in the State of California without the prior approval of the State Athletic Commission."
We made it boys. California sent us a Cease and Desist for "UNSANCTIONED HUMAN VERSUS HUMANOID ROBOT CAGE FIGHT" https://t.co/cw2jjl1aNV
— CIX 🦾 (@cixliv) September 30, 2026
Not sure if that throws any wrench in the future event plans of REK, or if maybe they were hoping for this kind of publicity all along. Since going up two weeks ago, the YouTube video above has garnered 8.2 million views.
Maybe that's enough to sell some robots, and/or sell some tickets to future robot-vs-robot matches.
Next up: We may be seeing new laws being written about when a humanoid robot is allowed to drop-kick or mortally injure an intruder in one's home, once more people start buying more of these things.

sources.text:
California officials pull plug on human-versus-robot cage matches
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Fun’s over.
California officials are calling foul on a company hosting man vs. robot cage fights in the state. Robot Entertainment Kombat hosted what it called the “world’s first human-robot fight” in San Francisco last month, shocking the internet.
A video of the fight shows the man, influencer Frankie LaPenna, clad in headgear, gloves, and kneepads facing off against a 6-foot-tall robot.
Sign up for the California Morning Report newsletter
The biggest news, opinion and culture shaping California right now.
Thanks for signing up!
The clip shows LaPenna and the robot exchanging blows, with the robot dramatically kicking the YouTuber to the ground several times. The fight racked up over 8 million views on YouTube, disturbing some.
“Welp, this is how it all begins,” one commenter joked.
“Some people will come back to this video after 20 or 30 years and will say “we could have stopped all this if we wanted to,” another user said.
“Fighting someone who can’t feel pain is genuinely terrifying,” a third user commented.
But state officials aren’t happy. Robot Entertainment received a cease and desist from the California State Athletic Commission following the fight, who ordered the company to stop the fights, or face a misdemeanor.
“We made it boys. California sent us a Cease and Desist for “UNSANCTIONED HUMAN VERSUS HUMANOID ROBOT CAGE FIGHT,” the company’s CEO Cix Liv said in an X post that included the letter.
But the letter wasn’t sent because people were facing off against robots, but rather because the company did not have the proper approval. According to the California business code, “no [full contact martial arts] event shall take place without the prior approval of the commission.”
Robot Entertainment Kombat has a fight scheduled in San Francisco for October 9, but this time, it’s robot vs. robot, no humans involved.

sources.news_title: Human Battles Humanoid Robots in Wild Viral Cage Fight
sources.text:
WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW
- Frankie LaPenna faced three humanoid robots during a cage fighting event staged by REK in San Francisco.
- Human pilots controlled the robots, while artificial intelligence assisted with balance and trained movement.
- REK says its modified EngineAI T800 machines can kick with up to 850 pounds of force.
- LaPenna was knocked down and injured his hand, but ultimately finished one bout with the robot’s head coming off.
Content creator Frankie LaPenna turned a robotics showcase into a viral spectacle by stepping inside a cage with humanoid machines.
In San Francisco, he faced three robots across a series of bouts that put a person directly against powerful metal opponents, as reported by Fox News.
The event was staged by REK, a robotics entertainment company that places remotely controlled humanoids into live combat events.
REK billed the showdown as the first cage fight between a human and a humanoid robot.

The footage attracting the most attention shows LaPenna advancing toward an EngineAI T800 and throwing several punches.
The robot responds with punches and kicks before a forceful shot sends LaPenna flying across the cage.
California sent a cease-and-desist letter to the tech startup REK after it hosted an unsanctioned cage match between a human and a humanoid robot https://t.co/P982DoFmzm
— Daily Loud (@DailyLoud) October 2, 2026
Its mechanical head and glowing red eyes give the machine a clear resemblance to The Terminator.
Beyond that theatrical appearance, however, the encounter offered a striking display of how humanoid robots can move, absorb contact, and remain balanced during physical combat.
This Could Be the Most Important Video Gun Owners Watch All Year
LaPenna first faced a smaller Unitree G1 before confronting two modified EngineAI T800 machines.
The T800 is built by Chinese robotics company EngineAI, which lists the standard model at about 5 feet 8 inches tall and roughly 165 to 187 pounds, depending on the version.
REK describes the modified T800 machines used in its fights as standing about 6 feet tall.
Placing machines of that size inside a confined fighting cage helped turn the footage into an especially intense demonstration.
The crucial detail is that the robots were not choosing to fight LaPenna independently.
REK technology partner Reflex Arc says human pilots operate the humanoids in real time through virtual reality equipment or a gamepad.
Artificial intelligence assists with balance and trained movement, while the pilot directs the robot’s actions.
Each punch and kick follows a human command, even though the machine must translate that instruction into physical movement while staying upright and recovering from contact.
According to REK CEO Cix Liv, LaPenna fought three robots during the event. He began with the smaller Unitree G1 and then moved on to the two modified T800 humanoids.
REK says its modified T800 machines can kick with up to 850 pounds of force.
That capability helps explain the dramatic sight of LaPenna being knocked down during one of the T800 bouts.
Liv said LaPenna recovered, knocked the robot off balance, and ultimately finished the fight with the machine’s head coming off.
REK has continued teasing additional footage, while the short clips circulating online show only part of the full sequence involving all three robots.
LaPenna initially wanted to fight without protective equipment, according to Liv, but REK insisted that he wear it.
He entered the cage in motorcycle protective gear and gloves, injured his hand while punching one robot and otherwise avoided serious injury.
REK has already been staging fights in which people remotely control humanoid robots against other humanoid robots.
The company also operates a simulator that lets players learn the controls before some receive an opportunity to pilot the physical machines.
Reflex Arc says REK’s first simulator championship produced 3,670 matches.
The winners were flown to San Francisco to control real robots at REK2 in August, using the same basic controls and trained balance system found in the simulator.
Humanoid robot combat had appeared before LaPenna entered the cage.
MORE NEWS: Drunken Michael Douglas Told Julia Roberts to Shove Her Golden Globe Where the Sun Don’t Shine
In 2025, four Unitree G1 humanoids controlled by human operators competed in a boxing tournament in China that featured punches, kicks, and knockdowns.
Other humanoids have played soccer without human control, rallied on a tennis court and kicked soccer balls hard enough to leave visible dents in a wall.
REK’s event pushed the spectacle in another direction by letting a human participant experience the machines’ physical strength directly.
Behind the Terminator styling and social media theatrics was a substantial robotics demonstration.
Machines weighing as much as about 187 pounds remained balanced in a restricted space, absorbed contact and executed forceful movements under human control.
The robots did not independently decide to attack, but their ability to carry out a pilot’s commands made the danger tangible.
LaPenna’s knockdown, hand injury, and protective gear showed that remote control does not make trading blows with a heavy humanoid machine harmless.

sources.news_title: YouTuber Fights Humanoid Robots in Unsanctioned MMA Bout
sources.text:
In a collision of some of the most terrifying elements of modern society, a YouTube and TikTok influencer has fought a series of humanoid robots in unsanctioned MMA bouts.
As Tom's Hardware reports, the farcical matchup was pure spectacle, with the main event robot sporting a Terminator-style face. However, it resulted in the California State Athletic Commission issuing a cease-and-desist letter to the organizers for promoting and participating in a boxing or martial arts contest without a license.
The Rek Humanoid Robot Fighting League is a fighting organization that hosts humanoid robot versus robot brawls in an undersized MMA cage. It's also developing a VR game in the same vein, but it drew spectators and headlines alike last month when it pitted a flesh-and-blood human against a trio of its robotic designs.
Representing humanity in the matchup was YouTube and TikTok influencer Frankie LaPenna, who, as far as I can tell, has limited traditional martial arts training. Regardless, he was pitted against robots built for MMA and managed to hold his own, at least against the smaller models.
    
        This Tweet is currently unavailable. It might be loading or has been removed.
    
In the latter fights, though, where he at one point squared off with a 6-foot-tall Terminator-esque design, he faced much stiffer competition. In some isolated clips of the event, the robot sends him flying across the cage with a push kick, and in another, connects with a head-kick, though LaPenna blocked it.
LaPenna got in a few licks, scoring some clean shots to the robot's head. Reportedly LaPenna was able to take the win across all fights, only losing one round, which is perhaps more of an indictment of the robot technology than it is a success for LaPenna himself.
    
        This Tweet is currently unavailable. It might be loading or has been removed.
    
Rek was clearly pleased with the promotion, though, and celebrated on social media when it received a cease-and-desist letter for the unsanctioned bout. It will now likely take the enterprise to other states where the licensing for combat sports is more favorable, though you have to wonder how any state would handle a serious injury to a human competitor in such a scenario.
Rek may have more control over the proceedings than its promotion lets on. While the robots are fully functional and perform all the moves they showcase, the main Rek show features two human controllers using the robots to battle one another, so this is merely an extension of that.
Still, it's a clear showcase of advances in robotics technology. It was only a few years ago that Boston Dynamics' robots jumping onto boxes was impressive. Now they're capable of knocking YouTubers on their butts. Perhaps it's payback for all those years of push-tests.

sources.news_title: Human vs humanoid robot cage fight goes viral
sources.text:
We've watched humanoid robots play soccer, run races and even fight other robots. Now, content creator Frankie LaPenna has taken things in a much wilder direction by stepping into a cage to fight them himself.
The event was staged by REK, a robotics entertainment company that puts remotely controlled humanoids into live combat events. In San Francisco, LaPenna faced three robots in a series of bouts, including two full-size EngineAI T800s, as part of what REK billed as the first human-versus-humanoid robot cage fight.
The viral footage getting most of the attention comes from one of those T800 fights. LaPenna moves toward the robot and throws several punches. The machine fires back with punches and kicks before one shot sends him flying across the cage. And if the robot looks like it walked straight out of "The Terminator," that was clearly the point. But the bigger story here is what these machines can actually do, who was controlling them and how much of the fighting was really driven by AI.

The bigger robots were modified EngineAI T800s
After facing a smaller Unitree G1, LaPenna went up against two modified EngineAI T800s, built by Chinese robotics company EngineAI. EngineAI lists the standard T800 at about 5 feet 8 inches tall and roughly 165 to 187 pounds, depending on the version. REK describes the modified machines used in its fights as about 6 feet tall. For the event, REK also gave the T800 a much more intimidating look. The mechanical head and glowing red eyes lean heavily into "The Terminator" theme. Put a machine that size inside a fighting cage and you can see why the video grabbed so much attention.
There was a person controlling the robot
Here's the big thing to know about this fight: there was a human behind the controls. REK's technology partner Reflex Arc says pilots operate the humanoids in real time using VR gear or a gamepad. AI helps with balance and trained movement, while the human pilot directs the action. So when you see a T800 throw a punch or launch a kick, the robot is carrying out the pilot's commands. It is not independently deciding how to fight LaPenna. That still leaves plenty to be impressed by because the machine has to stay upright, recover from contact and turn those commands into real physical movement inside the cage.
HUMANOID ROBOT VIDEOS SHOW MACHINES LASHING OUT
Frankie LaPenna actually fought three robots
The viral clip getting most of the attention only shows part of what happened that night. According to REK CEO Cix Liv, LaPenna faced three robots during the event. He reportedly started against a smaller Unitree G1 before moving on to two modified EngineAI T800 humanoids. REK says its modified T800 machines can kick with up to 850 pounds of force, which helps explain why the footage looks so intense.
LaPenna was knocked down during one of the T800 bouts, but Liv said he recovered, knocked the robot off balance and ultimately ended the fight with the robot's head coming off. REK has continued teasing more footage, and the short clips circulating online still do not show the full sequence of all three bouts. So what most people are seeing online is only one part of the event.
The fight took a physical toll on LaPenna
The physical side of the fight became pretty clear once LaPenna started trading punches with the robots. Liv said LaPenna originally wanted to fight without protective equipment, but REK insisted that he wear it. He ultimately entered the cage in motorcycle-style protective gear and gloves. According to Liv, LaPenna injured his hand while punching one of the robots but otherwise avoided a serious injury. Even with a human controlling the machine remotely, LaPenna was still trading blows with a heavy metal robot capable of putting real force behind its movements.
REK is betting on robot fighting as entertainment
REK has been building toward this kind of event for a while. The company stages live fights where people remotely control humanoid robots against other humanoid robots. It also has a simulator that lets players learn the controls before some get the chance to pilot the real machines. Reflex Arc says REK's first simulator championship generated 3,670 matches, with the winners flown to San Francisco to pilot real robots at REK2 in August. The simulator uses the same basic controls and trained balance system as the physical robots. That helps explain where REK is going with all of this. The idea is to take something that feels like a video game and put it into a real fighting cage with actual humanoid robots. Then LaPenna stepped inside and raised the stakes by putting a person on the other side.
LET'S LOOK BACK ON THE BEST MOMENTS (READ: CRASHES) FROM THE WORLD HUMANOID ROBOT GAMES
We've seen robot fighting before
Robot combat itself is nothing new, and we've been following that evolution closely. In 2025, four Unitree G1 humanoids fought in a boxing-style tournament in China. Those machines were also controlled by human operators, and the matches included punches, kicks and knockdowns. We have also watched humanoid robots play soccer without human control, rally on a tennis court and kick soccer balls hard enough to leave visible dents in a wall. REK's event takes that progression in a different direction. This time, the person sharing the cage with the machine can actually feel what happens when that robotic strength comes back at them.
What this human vs humanoid robot fight really shows
Strip away the Terminator head and the social media theatrics, and there is a pretty remarkable robotics demonstration underneath it. The larger T800s weigh as much as about 187 pounds, yet they can stay balanced in a confined fighting area, absorb contact and execute punches and kicks under human control.
The hardware is clearly becoming more capable. Compare today's humanoids with the awkward walking robots we were watching only a few years ago, and the change is dramatic. And something tells me Frankie LaPenna will not be the last person crazy enough to climb into the cage with one.
Kurt's key takeaways
I've watched humanoid robots do some pretty wild things, but seeing one kick a person across a cage definitely got my attention. The big thing to remember is that there was still a human pilot behind the controls. These robots were not independently deciding how to fight LaPenna. AI helped with balance and trained movement while a person directed the action in real time. What stands out to me is how quickly the physical side of this technology is advancing. These machines can stay upright through contact, recover and put some serious force behind their movements. REK even required LaPenna to wear protective gear before sending him into the cage. It makes for a viral video, but there is a more serious side to this, too. As humanoid robots become stronger and more capable, we are going to have to think carefully about who is controlling them, what safeguards are in place and where this kind of power should be used.

sources.news_title: Humanoid robots pummel YouTuber in cage matches, California tells startup to stop the fights
sources.text:
WTF?! You might think there are plenty of reasons why a real person shouldn't fight a humanoid robot in a cage match, but it happened anyway. The state of California wasn't pleased about this and has now sent a cease-and-desist letter to the robotics startup behind the event, telling it to stop holding these unsanctioned matches.
Last month, YouTuber Frankie LaPenna fought three different robots from REK, including a distinctly Terminator-like machine. At one point, the robot gave LaPenna a brutal kick to the face that sent him into the side of the cage, while another kick to the stomach sent the influencer flying onto his back. A different robot also put LaPenna on the ground with a fast series of punches to the face. It's all a bit concerning, really, though the child-like robot didn't put up much of a fight.
The California State Athletic Commission was also concerned about the event. It sent a cease-and-desist letter on September 30, demanding that REK stop hosting, promoting or sponsoring these fights.
REK CEO Cix Liv proudly shared the letter on X, writing that "we made it boys."
 – CIX 🦾 (@cixliv) September 30, 2026
The letter notes that any boxing or mixed martial arts contest, match, or exhibition, involving any human in the state of California, must first have approval from the California State Athletic Commission.
The letter adds that Business and Professions Codes section 18870 and 18878 make it a misdemeanor to promote or participate in a boxing or martial arts contest, match, or exhibition involving any human without a license.
Liv's unlikely to be too worried about the letter: don't be surprised if the fights simply move to another state or country. The free promotion will probably help, too.
Away from the legal ramifications, the fights illustrate just how quickly humanoid robots are advancing. It wasn't too long ago when a slight push from a human would have sent one of these machines sprawling to the floor and flopping around like a fish out of water. Video of the robots pounding the crap out of LaPenna looks like one of those pre-apocalypse news reports you'd find in an RPG about an AI that destroys the world.
There have been several reports recently about the military investigating use cases for humanoid robots. The US Army just named five companies as winners of the xTechHumanoid competition, which looks at ways these machines can be utilized in future military operations. One of the robots developed by a winner looks like it should be carrying a laser rifle and already has ballistic protection.
More recently, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced the creation of a new military command designed to expand the use of autonomous and robotic capabilities across the US armed forces.
It's not just the US, either. China is preparing humanoid robots for combat as it moves them from labs to military training grounds.

sources.news_title: Government Officials Order the Robot Cage Fights to Stop, Organizers Say
sources.text:
In mid-September, a new company called Robot Entertainment Kombat hosted what it claimed was the first-ever human-on-robot cage fight in California.
The whole thing was more WWE than “Real Steel” — behind the scenes, the robot was controlled by a human handler, and its strikes were sold wrastlin’-style by the dramatic human performer it “fought.”
Regardless of the authenticity, the California State Athletic Commission have apparently sent the organizers a cease and desist order, addressed to “all persons holding, promoting, advertising or sponsoring unsanctioned human versus humanoid robot cage fight[s].”
Using the letter to drum up some buzz on social media, Robot Entertainment Kombat founder Cix Liv seemed happy just to have the attention.
“We made it boys,” he wrote.
As per the letter he posted, the organizers were ordered to immediately stop hosting and promoting human-robot cage fights, or else face a misdemeanor charge.
In its letter, the Athletic Commission didn’t appear to take issue with the human-robot bouts per se, but with the organizers’ failure to secure the required permits.
That may be a distinction without a difference, however, as the Athletic Commission cited California business code which states that “no [full contact martial arts] event shall take place without the prior approval of the commission,” meaning the agency could simply withhold approval and veto a human-robot cage fight on a case-by-case basis — likely without ever having to explicitly declare such an event explicitly verboten.

sources.news_title: California Sends Angry Letter Over Viral Robot Vs Human Fight In San Francisco
sources.text:
The state of Califonia does not approve of humans fighting robots inside a cage.
Two weeks ago, influencer Frankie Lapenna faced off against a robot developed by REK, a San Francisco-based tech company that hosts remote-controlled bot fights.
The fight was held in San Francisco and the video went viral on social media.
“World’s first human vs 6ft terminator robot fight. Is the end near? Or do we still stand a chance?” Lapenna wrote on TikTok.
We just made history with the first Human VS Terminator robot fight.
Frankie LaPenna gave it his all 🥊 More fight footage coming soon! pic.twitter.com/iADpv9d8Wg
— REK (@REK) September 20, 2026
The California State Athletic Commission, which oversees combat sports in the state, sent an angry cease-and-desist in hopes of preventing future human vs. robot fights.
ALL PERSONS HOLDING, PROMOTING, ADVERTISING OR SPONSORING UNSANCTIONED HUMAN VERSUS HUMANOID ROBOT CAGE FIGHT (MOST RECENT EVENT SEPTEMBER 18, 2026, SAN FRANCISCO)
PLEASE TAKE NOTICE that you and each of you are hereby ordered to cease and desist from: (1) holding, promoting or advertising any boxing or mixed martial arts contest match, or exhibition, involving any human in the State of California without the prior approval of the California State Athletic Commission, or (2) engaging in the promotion of, or participation in, a boxing or martial arts contest, match, or exhibition involving any human without a license pursuant to Business and Professions Code section 18640.
PLEASE TAKE FURTHER NOTICE that Business and Professions Code sections 18870 and 18878 make it a misdemeanor for a person or promoter who is required to be licensed by the State Athletic Commission to directly or indirectly hold, aid or abet, or attempt to hold, aid or abet the holding of, any contest, match or exhibition without first having obtained a license or permit therefor from the State Athletic Commission or to otherwise violate any provision of the State Athletic Commission Act.
We made it boys. California sent us a Cease and Desist for “UNSANCTIONED HUMAN VERSUS HUMANOID ROBOT CAGE FIGHT” pic.twitter.com/cw2jjl1aNV
— CIX 🦾 (@cixliv) September 30, 2026

sources.news_title: California Sends Cease and Desist to Fight Promotion for “Unsanctioned” Human vs. Humanoid Robot Bout
sources.text:
The fight billed as the world’s first human vs. humanoid robot cage match went viral in the days after the bout took place in California on September 18 under the Robot Entertainment Kombat (REK) banner. Now, however, the unusual spectacle that amazed users online has caught the attention of the California State Athletic Commission, which has ordered the promotion to stop holding similar events or face punitive action.
Watch What’s Trending Now!
The CEO and founder of REK, CIX (Cix Liv), shared online the official cease-and-desist order, dated 23rd September, from the CSAC executive officer Andy Foster, while celebrating the infamous milestone.
“We made it, boys,” Cix Liv wrote on X alongside a picture of the CSAC notice. “California sent us a Cease and Desist for ‘UNSANCTIONED HUMAN VERSUS HUMANOID ROBOT CAGE FIGHT.’”
The notice refers to the promotion’s first human vs. humanoid matchup in San Francisco on September 18.
The event featured 29-year-old internet influencer and content creator Frankie LaPenna taking on a six-foot-tall EngineAI T800 humanoid robot under the REK banner.
According to the CSAC notice, REK did not obtain the required license or sanctions from the commission before holding the event. The commission cited Business and Professions Code section 18640, which defines a combat match strictly as a physical harm contest between two or more persons, leaving robotic combat outside existing athletic commission definitions.
That means what may have looked like a futuristic experiment to viewers online still fell under the commission’s regulatory authority because an actual human fighter was involved.
The CSAC has now ordered REK to stop holding similar events. The notice also warns of potential penalties if the promotion continues to violate the relevant provisions of California law.
For REK, the notice creates a big problem for a promotion that has built its identity around increasingly unconventional combat-sports events.
For a while now, Robot Entertainment Kombat has primarily focused on robot-vs.-robot competitions.
In September 2025, the promotion held an event featuring bipedal robots roughly 4.5 feet tall, with UFC fighters including Jessica-Rose Clark and Hyder Amil attending to test some of the machines.
The latest event, however, took things a step further.
Instead of putting two robots against each other, REK placed a human inside the cage with a six-foot, 200-pound humanoid robot dubbed “Rekbot,” a machine modeled after Arnold Schwarzenegger’s iconic Terminator character.
LaPenna managed to land several strikes during the fight, but the robot eventually returned fire with a powerful push kick that sent the influencer flying. Footage showed LaPenna slamming hard into the canvas and the plastic-lined Plexiglas cage wall.
The sequence made for a dramatic moment, although the influencer did not appear to suffer a serious injury from the exchange.
REK subsequently celebrated the bout as a milestone for the promotion.
“We just made history with the first Human VS Terminator robot fight,” REK wrote on X. “Le Penna gave it his all.”
The event certainly generated attention online. However, the commission’s notice makes clear that the fight promotion violated state law under Code section 18640 by holding an event involving an actual human without prior approval from the commission, rendering the event unsanctioned.
As of now, the CSAC has formally demanded that the promotion stop holding such events in the future through a “cease and desist” notice. But if the promotion is found in violation of the state law again, it could invite punishment under Section 412, which entails financial penalties between $100 and $1,000 and imprisonment ranging from 30 days up to a year.
For now, there is no indication that REK’s robot-vs.-robot events are necessarily subject to the same issue. The commission’s action only centers on the inclusion of an actual human combatant.
That distinction could determine what comes next for the league.
REK has already shown that it wants to push combat sports into territory few traditional promotions have explored. But after California’s athletic commission stepped in, the organization will now have to figure out where, and under what regulatory framework, it can continue experimenting with human vs. humanoid competition. So, either they must stop holding such events altogether or move to a state where the legislature is not as stringent as it is in California.
